name: Blue light blocking glasses

card.summary: Amber or tinted glasses worn in the evening to reduce blue light and protect melatonin; small trials exist, reviews of eye-health claims are mixed.
card.note: Reviews cited by Grokipedia report limited evidence for eye strain and sleep benefits in general populations.

quick.overview:
Blue light blocking glasses filter part of the blue spectrum (about 400 to 500 nm) emitted by screens and LEDs. In sleep circles, amber-tinted versions are worn in the evening on the idea that blue light suppresses melatonin and delays sleep.

Small trials have tested evening use in teenagers, healthy adults and people with delayed sleep phase disorder. Broader reviews of eye strain and sleep claims are described as mixed.
quick.mechanism: Lenses use dye-based tints, commonly amber or yellow, or thin-film interference coatings to absorb or reflect part of the blue wavelengths. The circadian system is most sensitive to blue light, which is the basis for the evening-use rationale.
quick.risks: No notable harms are reported for ordinary use. A 2007 paper discussed safety considerations for wearing them in shift workers, who need to stay alert.

lead: Blue light blocking glasses are eyewear designed to filter part of the blue spectrum, typically 400 to 500 nm, from screens, LED lighting and sunlight. Lenses use amber or yellow dye-based tints or interference coatings, and are available with or without prescription [1].

Proponents of evening use, including users interested in sleep optimisation, say that blue light suppresses melatonin and delays the body clock, so filtering it after dark protects sleep. Small trials have tested this, including studies in teenagers [2], people with delayed sleep phase disorder [3] and healthy adults [4].

Broader assessments differ. Grokipedia reports that Cochrane reviews and the American Academy of Ophthalmology found no clear benefit for eye strain or sleep from blue-light-filtering lenses in general use [1].
infobox: Dye-based tints (amber, yellow) and interference coatings [1]
Rose in the 2010s and during the COVID-19 pandemic [1]

paras: Lenses are commonly polycarbonate or Trivex. Dye-based tints in amber or yellow absorb part of the blue range, while interference filters use thin-film coatings to reflect specific wavelengths [1]. Clear lenses that block a small fraction of blue light are marketed for screen use, while darker amber lenses filter more and are marketed for evening wear [1].

Grokipedia traces the modern products to the early 2000s and cites the founding of Gunnar Optiks in 2007, with popularity surging in the 2010s and during the COVID-19 pandemic [1]. This account comes from an AI-generated source and has not been independently verified here.

A 2015 study investigated whether blue-light-blocking glasses worn in the evening counter the alerting effects of LED screen exposure in male teenagers [2]. A 2016 four-week open-label trial in patients with delayed sleep phase disorder had them wear amber glasses from 21:00 until bedtime and reported advanced circadian rhythms [3]. A 2021 randomised controlled trial examined evening blue light blocking glasses on subjective and objective sleep in healthy adults [4], and a 2021 study examined pre-bedtime blue-light exposure and the ratio of deep sleep in healthy young men [5].

A 2020 paper reported that reducing evening blue light advanced sleep and melatonin as a strategy against social jetlag [6], and another 2020 paper examined evening blue light filtration as part of cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia [7]. A 2014 case report described a hospitalised patient in a manic state whose sleep regularity and symptoms improved with blue-blocking orange-tinted glasses [8], and a 2022 systematic review covered sleep and circadian interventions in bipolar disorder [9]. A 2007 paper discussed safety considerations for use in shift workers [10].

Grokipedia reports that Cochrane reviews of blue-light-filtering lenses found no significant reduction in visual performance problems, sleep disturbance or macular degeneration risk, and that the American Academy of Ophthalmology states there is no scientific evidence that screen blue light damages eyes [1]. No studies were found testing the glasses for appearance outcomes.
